elements.id-string-7: In this paper, we introduce DR-HAI -- a novel argumentation-based framework designed to extend model reconciliation approaches, commonly used in explainable AI planning, for enhanced human-AI interaction.
elements.id-string-8: By adopting a multi-shot reconciliation paradigm and not assuming a-priori knowledge of the human user's model, DR-HAI enables interactive reconciliation to address knowledge discrepancies between an explainer and an explainee.
elements.id-string-9: We formally describe the operational semantics of DR-HAI, provide theoretical guarantees related to termination and success, and empirically evaluate its efficacy.
elements.id-string-10: Our findings suggest that DR-HAI offers a promising direction for fostering effective human-AI interactions.
elements.id-string-13: The significance of creating AI agents that can establish trust and accountability by interacting with human users is constantly increasing.
elements.id-string-14: This is the central idea behind the field of \emph{explainable AI planning} (XAIP), which aims to design agents that are transparent and explainable by considering the human user's knowledge, preferences, and values \cite{sreedharan2022explainable}.
elements.id-string-15: A crucial aspect in XAIP is the human-AI interaction, where the AI agent is expected to communicate effectively with humans to enhance their understanding and address their concerns.
elements.id-string-16: Most research efforts within XAIP have been placed on (sequential) decision-making tasks involving an agent and a human user, and the goal is to make the agent's decisions explainable and transparent to the human user when those decisions appear inexplicable to them.
elements.id-string-17: While there have been a plethora of approaches to solve XAIP from different perspectives~\cite{chakraborti2020emerging}, a process called \emph{model reconciliation} has garnered growing interest \cite{chakraborti2017plan, sreedharan2018handling, ijcai2019, son2021model, vas21, vasileioulogic}.
elements.id-string-18: In model reconciliation, it is assumed that the agent and the human user each have their own (mental) models of the task, and the need for explainability arises due to some knowledge asymmetry between these two models that makes the agent's decisions inexplicable with respect to the human user's model.
elements.id-string-19: A solution in model reconciliation is then an \emph{explanation} (technically, a minimal set of model updates) from the agent to the human user such that the agent's decisions become explicable to the human user.
elements.id-string-20: Despite the growing popularity of model reconciliation approaches, we identify two limitations: (1)~It is commonly assumed that \emph{the agent possesses the human user's model a-priori} in order to anticipate their goals and predict how its decision will be perceived by them.
elements.id-string-21: This may lead to incorrect assumptions about the human user's knowledge and preferences, and consequently to unsatisfactory explanations.
elements.id-string-22: (2)~Most model reconciliation approaches are formulated around \emph{a single-shot reconciliation paradigm}, that is, they focus on generating a single, albeit comprehensive, explanation that is presented all at once.
elements.id-string-23: While this type of reconciliation can be useful when the human user needs to quickly understand a decision or when the underlying task is relatively simple, it may fail to work for more complex decisions and tasks that require a more detailed understanding from the human user, especially when there is substantial knowledge discrepancy between the agent and user models.
elements.id-string-24: Our proposal in this paper addresses these two limitations by proposing a new model reconciliation framework that is formulated around \emph{a multi-shot reconciliation paradigm with no assumptions about an a-priori human user model}.
elements.id-string-25: Particularly, we introduce the notion of \emph{dialectical reconciliation},\footnote{Dialectic refers to a discourse between individuals with differing or conflicting views to determine truth via logical argumentation.} and propose a framework aimed at enhancing human-AI interaction by helping the human user understand the agent's decisions, and, ultimately, the agent's behavior from the perspective of the agent.
elements.id-string-26: Note that the goal is not to convince the user to agree and accept the decisions of the agent, as the user may end up disagreeing with the decisions despite understanding why the agent made those decisions.
elements.id-string-27: We believe that these kinds of interactions are likely to grow as AI agents play more pervasive roles in our daily life, and we seek to understand the reasons for its behavior.
elements.id-string-28: Our framework, called \emph{Dialectical Reconciliation in Human-AI Interactions} (DR-HAI), is formalized in a game-theoretic manner, wherein an explainee agent (e.g.,~a human user) and an explainer agent (e.g.,~an AI agent) make moves in a game governed by rules that define the appropriateness of their utterances.
elements.id-string-29: We describe the \emph{operational semantics} of DR-HAI, that is, the underlying mechanism for selecting appropriate moves, with the use of \emph{logic-based argumentation} \cite{besnard2001logic}, thus making it possible for the participants to express their conflicting views through formal arguments, and, as such, reconcile their differences.
elements.id-string-30: Finally, we discuss the concept of explainee understanding in the context of human-AI interactions, and present a simple method for approximating it.
elements.id-string-31: In short, our thesis in this paper is premised as follows:
elements.id-string-33: \emph{DR-HAI enables effective human-AI interactions for tasks involving substantial knowledge discrepancies between the explainee and explainer by improving the explainee's understanding of the explainer's decisions and behavior through dialectical reconciliation.}
elements.id-string-34: In the next section, we report some empirical findings from a human-user study aimed at examining the roles of single-shot reconciliation versus dialectical reconciliation in fostering human-AI interaction and understanding.
elements.id-string-36: We conducted a study involving a simulated scenario where a human user is presented with the task of troubleshooting an AI home assistant robot named "Roomie" that appears to be disconnected from the internet.
elements.id-string-37: In this scenario, the user is given a set of prompts to help them diagnose the problem, such as checking the associated mobile app, confirming Roomie's connection to the charging base, verifying Roomie's connection to the internet via a wired connector, and noting a flashing light next to the LAN port.
elements.id-string-38: However, the situation is not as straightforward as it seems, and the user is faced with several complications that hinder their ability to resolve the issue.
elements.id-string-39: These include an outdated mobile app, an expired license for the wired connection, and a low battery indicated by the flashing light.
elements.id-string-40: These obstacles create a realistic scenario for the user to navigate, as they must interact with Roomie to understand the underlying issues in order to get it up and running again.
elements.id-string-41: Overall, this study provides a valuable opportunity to explore how humans interact with AI systems in real-world situations, and how they approach troubleshooting and problem-solving when faced with unexpected obstacles.

elements.id-string-44: Participants were introduced to the problem through a narrative dialogue that explained the scenario's premise and known information.
elements.id-string-45: After posing the initial query ``Why are you disconnected?'', participants were divided into two groups:
elements.id-string-46: \textbf{Single-Shot (SSR)}: Group 1 received a single-shot model reconciliation explanation, where the human model was assumed to include the information provided during the scenario's introduction.
elements.id-string-47: The explanations were computed using a state-of-the-art solver~\cite{vas21}.\footnote{We used the implementations provided by the authors.}
elements.id-string-48: \textbf{DR-HAI}: Group 2 interacted with DR-HAI's explanations, choosing from four unique questions (counterarguments to Roomie's responses) in a game-like format.

elements.id-string-50: Upon completing their interaction with Roomie, participants were asked four multiple-choice questions to evaluate their understanding of the issues, generating a comprehension score.
elements.id-string-51: They also responded to four Likert-scale questions (1: strongly disagree, 5: strongly agree) to gauge their satisfaction with the interaction and explanations, resulting in a satisfaction score.

elements.id-string-108: We now introduce the \emph{Dialectical Reconciliation in Human-AI Interactions} (DR-HAI) framework.
elements.id-string-109: In this framework, two agents engage in a dialogue, with one agent taking on the role of an \emph{explainer} (denoted by index~$r$) and the other an \emph{explainee} (denoted by index~$e$).
elements.id-string-110: Recall that the scope of the dialogue is to help the explainee \emph{understand} the decisions made by the explainer \emph{from the perspective of the explainer}.
elements.id-string-111: Using our user study scenario as an example, the goal is to enable the human user to understand why Roomie thinks that it is disconnected from the internet, independent of whether Roomie is truly disconnected or not.
elements.id-string-112: We use $\phi$ to represent an explainer's decision and $\varphi$ to represent the set of all decisions the explainee seeks to understand.
elements.id-string-113: In other words, DR-HAI's primary high-level goal is for the explainee to understand the explainer's reasoning, which leads to $\varphi$.
elements.id-string-114: Three critical assumptions underlie the DR-HAI framework:
elements.id-string-115: \textbf{Agent knowledge bases:} The explainer is associated with a knowledge base $KB_r$ that encodes its own knowledge of the underlying task.
elements.id-string-116: The explainee is associated with knowledge base $KB_e$ that encodes \emph{their approximation of the explainer's knowledge}, which can be $\emptyset$.
elements.id-string-117: No agent has a-priori access to the other's knowledge base.
elements.id-string-118: \textbf{Explainee queries:} The explainee has a set of possible queries $\varphi$ for the explainer,
elements.id-string-120: The explainee initiates a dialogue with an initial query $\phi_1$.
elements.id-string-121: \textbf{Commitment stores:} Each agent has access to a \emph{commitment store}, defined as a tuple $CS_x = \langle CS_x^1, \ldots, CS_x^t \rangle$ $(x\in \{e, r\})$, that stores each agent's utterances throughout the dialogue.
elements.id-string-122: Both agents have access to each other's commitment stores.\footnote{A commitment store is akin to a ``chat log" and is used to store all the information that has been exchanged between the agents in the dialogue.}
elements.id-string-123: With these assumptions in place, the primary goal of DR-HAI can be formulated as follows:
elements.id-string-124: \emph{Given an explainer agent with $KB_r$, an explainee agent with $KB_e$, and a set of queries $\varphi$ s.t., for all $\phi \in \varphi$, $KB_e \not \models \phi$ (or $KB_e \models \neg \phi$) and $KB_r \models \phi$, the goal of DR-HAI is to \emph{enable} $KB_e \models \phi$ through logic-based argumentation.}
elements.id-string-125: A critical aspect of this formulation is effectively enabling $KB_e \models \phi$ during the dialogue between explainee and explainer.
elements.id-string-126: At a high level, we aim to find a way to help the explainee transition from a state of not understanding a decision $\phi$ (i.e.,~$KB_e \not \models \phi$ or $KB_e \models \neg \phi$) to a state of understanding the decision (i.e.,~$KB_e \models \phi$).
elements.id-string-127: Our thesis in this paper is that a natural way of achieving this transition is through an argumentation-based dialogue that facilitates \emph{dialectical reconciliation}.
elements.id-string-128: In the DR-HAI framework, dialectical reconciliation is the process of resolving inconsistencies, misunderstandings, and gaps in knowledge between explainee and explainer.
elements.id-string-129: It relies on the exchange of arguments, conflicts, and other dialogue moves that allow the agents to collaboratively construct a shared understanding of the decisions in question.
elements.id-string-130: To successfully achieve dialectical reconciliation, the agents follow certain dialogue protocols that guide their interaction:
elements.id-string-131: Establish a clear dialogue structure, including the use of \emph{locutions} that define permissible speech acts and turn-taking mechanisms.
elements.id-string-132: Engage in a cooperative and collaborative manner, with both agents focusing on the shared goal of improving the explainee's understanding.
elements.id-string-133: Employing argumentation techniques, such as offering counterexamples or pointing out logical inconsistencies, to constructively challenge each other's positions and beliefs.
elements.id-string-134: By adhering to these protocols and engaging in dialectical reconciliation, the explainer can help the explainee iteratively refine their knowledge base, ultimately converging on a shared understanding that enables $KB_e \models \phi$ for all decisions in $\varphi$.
elements.id-string-136: We now introduce the dialectical reconciliation dialogue type, drawing upon Hamblin's dialectical games framework \cite{hamblin1970fallacies,hamblin1971mathematical}.
elements.id-string-137: Here, a dialogue is viewed as a game-theoretic interaction, where utterances are treated as moves governed by rules that define their applicability.
elements.id-string-138: In this context, moves consist of a set of \emph{locutions}, which determine the types of permissible utterances agents can make.
elements.id-string-139: To align with the goals of DR-HAI, we define the following set of locutions:
elements.id-string-141: The $query$ locution enables the explainee to ask the explainer for an argument that supports the explainee's query.
elements.id-string-142: The $support$ locution allows the explainer to provide such an argument that supports the explainee's query.
elements.id-string-143: The $refute$ locution permits both agents to present counterarguments, and the $agree$-$to$-$disagree$ locution allows both agents to acknowledge each other's utterances when no further queries or counterarguments are possible.
elements.id-string-144: We opt for an $agree$-$to$-$disagree$ locution instead of a simple $agree$ (or $accept$) locution as the goal of DR-HAI is not to convince the explainee about $\varphi$ but to help them understand $\varphi$.
elements.id-string-145: An $agree$-$to$-$disagree$ locution reflects this flexibility, where agents do not have to agree with each other; they only have to acknowledge each other's utterances and understand each other's perspectives.
elements.id-string-146: Furthermore, we impose two restrictions: (1)~The $query$ locution is only available to the explainee, and (2)~The $support$ locution is only available to the explainer.
elements.id-string-147: These restrictions are reasonable given the goal of DR-HAI; future work will explore relaxing them.
elements.id-string-148: Locutions are typically instantiated with specific formulae that make up the range of possible \emph{dialogue moves} $m_t$:

elements.id-string-152: We now define the concept of a DR-HAI dialogue.
elements.id-string-153: A DR-HAI dialogue requires that the first move must always be a $query$ locution from the explainee, and the agents take turns making and receiving moves.
elements.id-string-155: A \emph{DR-HAI dialogue} $D$ is a sequence of moves $[m_1,\ldots, m_{|D|}]$ involving an explainee agent $e$ and an explainer agent $r$, and the following conditions hold:\squishenum[1.] $m_1 = \langle e, query, \Phi \rangle$ is the opening move of the dialogue made by the explainee.[2.] Each agent can make and receive only one move $m_t$ per timestep $t$.\squishend
elements.id-string-156: We refer to the explainee queries $\varphi$ made in the dialogue as the \emph{topic} of the dialogue.
elements.id-string-157: We use $\mathcal{D}$ to represent the set of all dialogues.
elements.id-string-158: A DR-HAI dialogue is \emph{terminated} at timestep $t$ if and only if the explainee cannot generate subsequent queries or counterarguments, that is, when the explainee utters the $agree$-$to$-$disagree$ locution.
elements.id-string-160: A DR-HAI dialogue $D$ is \emph{terminated} at timestep $t$ iff $m_t = \langle e, agree$-$to$-$disagree, \emptyset \rangle$ and $\nexists t'<t$ s.t.
elements.id-string-162: During the dialogue, the agents essentially decide which dialogue moves to make.
elements.id-string-163: An agent may have a specific objective in mind when making its decision, such as adhering to rationality principles, ending the dialogue quickly, or prolonging the dialogue as much as possible.
elements.id-string-164: The mechanism for deciding a move that takes this overall aim into account is called an \emph{agent strategy}.
elements.id-string-165: We can think of the agent strategy for an agent $x$ as a function $S_x$ that takes in its current dialogue $D$, knowledge base $KB_x$, next timestep $t$ and returns its next dialogue move.
elements.id-string-166: While agent strategies can take several forms (e.g.,~preference-based, probabilistic), for simplicity, we will consider the agents follow an ordered strategy.
elements.id-string-167: That is, $S_e(D, KB_e, t) = [refute$, $query$, $agree$-$to$-$disagree]$ and $S_r(D, KB_r, t) = [support$, $refute$, $agree$-$to$-$disagree]$, where the ordered lists show the priorities of dialogue moves for the explainee and explainer, respectively, at timestep $t > 1$.
elements.id-string-168: Finally, if the agents follow their agent strategies during the DR-HAI dialogue, and the dialogue does not continue after it has terminated, then we say that the DR-HAI dialogue is \emph{well-formed}.
elements.id-string-169: A DR-HAI dialogue $D$ is \emph{well-formed} iff it is terminated at timestep $t$ and, for all timesteps $1<t'<t$, $S_x(D', KB_x, t') = m_{t'}$ for each move $m_{t'}$ from agent $x$, where $D' \subseteq D$ consists of the first $|D'| = t' - 1$ moves from $D$.
elements.id-string-170: For the remainder of the paper, we assume that all DR-HAI dialogues are well-formed.

elements.id-string-610: In this section, we introduce the \textit{Dialectical Reconciliation via Structured Argumentative Dialogues} (DR-Arg) framework.
elements.id-string-611: We begin by discussing the key assumptions and components of the framework.
elements.id-string-613: The DR-Arg framework involves two agents engaging in a dialogue, with one agent taking on the role of an \textit{explainer} (denoted by index~$R$) and the other an \textit{explainee} (denoted by index~$E$).
elements.id-string-614: The goal of the dialogue is to \textit{help the explainee understand the decisions made by the explainer from the explainer's perspective}.
elements.id-string-615: We use $\phi$ to represent an explainer's decision and $\Phi$ to represent the set of all decisions the explainee seeks to understand.
elements.id-string-616: Three critical assumptions underlie our framework:
elements.id-string-618: \textbf{Agent Knowledge Bases:} The explainer is associated with a knowledge base $\KB_R$ that encodes its own knowledge of the underlying task.
elements.id-string-619: The explainee is associated with knowledge base $\KB_E$ that encodes \emph{their approximation of the explainer's knowledge}, which can be $\emptyset$.
elements.id-string-620: No agent has explicit access to the other agent's knowledge base.\textbf{Explainee Queries:} Initiated by the explainee, the dialogue starts with a \texttt{query} $\phi \in \Phi$, where $\KB_E \not \models \phi$ (or $\KB_E \models \neg \phi$) and $\KB_R \models \phi$.
elements.id-string-621: The explainee has the flexibility to generate subsequent queries dynamically as the dialogue progresses, reflecting their evolving understanding and the need for additional clarification.\textbf{Public Commitment Stores:} Both agents contribute to public \textit{commitment stores} that store their utterances throughout the dialogue, akin to a ``chat log".
elements.id-string-622: A commitment store for agent $x\in \{R, E\}$ is defined as $CS_x = ( CS_x^1, \ldots, CS_x^t )$, where $CS_x^t = \langle l(\gamma), A \rangle$ and $l(\gamma)$ is an instantiated locution (see next section) and $A$ the respective argument (can be empty) accompanying the locution.
elements.id-string-623: This feature allows to build more complex and contextually aware arguments.
elements.id-string-624: The main goal of the DR-Arg is formulated as follows:
elements.id-string-625: \emph{Given an explainer agent with $\KB_R$, an explainee agent with $\KB_E$, and a set of queries $\Phi$ such that, for all $\phi \in \Phi$, $\KB_E \not \models \phi$ (or $\KB_E \models \neg \phi$) and $\KB_R \models \phi$, the goal of DR-Arg is to \emph{enable} $\KB_E \models \phi$ through dialectical reconciliation.}
elements.id-string-626: A critical aspect of this formulation is successfully \textit{enabling} $\KB_E \models \phi$ during the dialogue between explainee and explainer.
elements.id-string-627: At a high level, we aim to find a way to help the explainee transition from a state of \textit{not understanding} a decision $\phi$ (i.e.,~$\KB_E \not \models \phi$ or $\KB_E \models \neg \phi$) to a state of \textit{understanding} the decision (i.e.,~$\KB_E \models \phi$).
elements.id-string-628: Our thesis is that a natural way of achieving this transition is through an argumentation-based dialogue that facilitates dialectical reconciliation, i.e., a \textit{dialectical reconciliation dialogue}.
elements.id-string-629: At a high level, a dialectical reconciliation dialogue is a process resolving inconsistencies, misunderstandings, and knowledge gaps between the explainer and the explainee.
elements.id-string-630: This is achieved through argument exchange and dialogue moves that collaboratively construct a shared understanding of the explainer's decisions.

elements.id-string-632: Following these protocols, the explainer helps the explainee iteratively refine their knowledge base, ultimately converging on a shared understanding that enables $\KB_E \models \phi$ for all decisions $\phi \in \Phi$.

elements.id-string-793: We present two forms of empirical evaluations -- a computational experiment and a human-user study.
elements.id-string-795: For our computational evaluation of DR-Arg, we utilize the following metrics to assess its performance:
elements.id-string-796: \textbf{Change in Similarity $\Delta \Sigma$:} The change in the similarity between $KB_E$ and $KB_R$ (for $a =0.5$), comparing their initial (pre-interaction) and final (post-interaction) levels.
elements.id-string-798: We created 16 unique pairs of $\KB_R$ and $\KB_E$ with sizes of $10^2 - 10^5$ by doing the following.
elements.id-string-799: (1)~We generated random inconsistent propositional KBs of varying sizes of $10^2 - 10^5$.
elements.id-string-800: (2)~We constructed $\KB_R$ by removing a minimal correction set (MCS) from the inconsistent KB to make them consistent.\footnote{A MCS is a $\subseteq$-minimal set of formulae whose removal renders an inconsistent KB consistent~\citep{marques-silva-ijcai13}.} (3)~To create $\KB_E$, we controlled the fraction of conflicts between the explainer and explainee with $c = |\KB_E| / |\KB_R|$.
elements.id-string-801: Specifically, starting with an empty $\KB_E$, we added formulae from MCS and, if needed, negations of random formulae from $\KB_R$ to meet the desired ratio.
elements.id-string-802: (4)~Lastly, to have KBs of approximately the same size and with some similarity between them, we added a $1-c$ fraction of formulae from $\KB_R$ to $\KB_E$, as long as $\KB_E$ remained satisfiable.
elements.id-string-803: For generating arguments and counterarguments, we used a standard method from the literature~\citep{besnard2010mus}.
elements.id-string-804: The dialogue topic comprised a single \texttt{query} $\phi$, created by finding a formula entailed by $\KB_R$ but not by $\KB_E$.
elements.id-string-805: This process ensured the \texttt{query} addressed the knowledge discrepancy between the explainer and explainee, allowing to simulate a dialectical reconciliation dialogue.

elements.id-string-847: Argumentation is often advocated as suitable for explanation, but there are very few studies of its suitability to humans.~In this paper, we presented DR-Arg, a novel framework utilizing (structured deductive) argumentation for performing dialectical reconciliation between an explainer and an explainee.
elements.id-string-848: We conducted a thorough evaluation ``in the wild'', with our computational and human-user study results attesting to the efficacy of our approach.~These findings highlight the potential of argumentation-based approaches in enhancing the human-AI interaction of AI systems, particularly in domains where explainability is crucial.
elements.id-string-849: Despite the promising aspects of our framework, it is important to acknowledge its limitations and potential areas for improvement.
elements.id-string-850: DR-Arg follows a fixed structure in presenting arguments and does not consider the effectiveness of personalizing the interactions according to the user's beliefs and preferences.
elements.id-string-851: DR-Arg also assumes seamless communication through well-defined dialogue moves, which may not reflect real-world complexities such as miscommunication or uncertainty.
elements.id-string-852: Finally, the current framework is limited to deductive argumentation and propositional logic, which may not be sufficient to express complex relationships and dependencies in real-world domains.
elements.id-string-853: To address these limitations, we suggest the following future directions: (1)~Develop an adaptive approach that tailors arguments to individual users' needs and preferences based on user feedback and prior interactions \cite{sreedharan2021using,vasileioua2023please}.
elements.id-string-854: In \citet{tang2024approximating}, we have taken a preliminary step towards this end by proposing a probabilistic framework to approximate human user models from argumentation-based dialogues; (2)~Integrate DR-Arg with large language models \cite{brown2020language} to translate formal arguments and logical structures into intuitive, natural language expressions, enhancing accessibility and user-friendliness while maintaining logical coherence; and (3)~Consider alternative structured argumentation frameworks, such as ABA \cite{bondarenko1997abstract,vcyras2016aba+} or probabilistic argumentation frameworks \cite{kohlas2003probabilistic,hunter2013probabilistic}, to enable more complex reasoning and argument generation for a wider range of real-world problems.
